# Insertional tendinopathies

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > General orthopedics > Insertional tendinopathies*

[Original Article Link](/library/vQ0ABf)

---

## Summary

Insertional tendinopathies are common disorders caused by repetitive strain on <u>tendons</u> at their point of origin or insertion on a bone. Insertional tendinopathies are most common in athletes and people who regularly perform repetitive movements (e.g., typing, assembly-line work). The Achilles, patellar, forearm, and <u>rotator cuff</u> <u>tendons</u> are most commonly affected. Insertional tendinopathies typically manifest with insidious onset of focal <u>pain</u> and tenderness and are associated with an increase in activity. Diagnosis is usually clinical. In cases of diagnostic uncertainty, <u>x-ray</u> is used to rule out bone pathology and is followed by either <u>ultrasound</u> or <u>MRI</u>. <u>Conservative management</u> leads to complete remission in most patients. For refractory symptoms, treatment options include <u>glucocorticoid</u> injections, <u>extracorporeal shock wave therapy</u>, and <u>surgery</u>.




This article covers <u>lateral epicondylitis</u>, <u>medial epicondylitis</u>, <u>iliotibial band syndrome</u>, <u>patellar tendinopathy</u>, and <u>Achilles tendinopathy</u>. <u>Rotator cuff tendinopathy</u>, <u>biceps tendinopathy</u>, and <u>greater trochanteric pain syndrome</u> are covered in other articles.

---

## Etiology

* Overuse or overload injury (repetitive, excessive strain), degeneration

* Skeletal abnormalities with strain on <u>tendons</u> (e.g., <u>genu varum</u>)

* Acute trauma (<u>laceration</u>, rupture)

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Occupation: athletes, workers who do manual <u>labor</u> or repetitive movements involving the same muscle

* Errors in physical training (e.g., sudden increase in exercise intensity, inadequate rest, hard/uneven training grounds, ill-fitting/inappropriate footwear)

* <u>Obesity</u>

* Previous <u>tendon</u> injuries

* Recent use of <u>fluoroquinolones</u>

---

## Pathophysiology

* Contraction of a <u>skeletal muscle</u> → transmission of force through the <u>tendon</u> to the bone at the point of <u>tendon</u> insertion

* Repetitive strain → microtrauma of the <u>tendon</u> → improper healing → <u>disorientation</u> of the <u>tendon</u>'s <u>collagen fibers</u> →  tendinopathy

* Hypovascularity → predisposition to <u>hypoxic</u> <u>tendon</u> degeneration





> [!TIP]
> Unlike in cases of tendinitis or <u>tenosynovitis</u>, inflammation plays a negligible role in the development of tendinopathy.

---

## Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow)

<u>Lateral epicondylitis</u> is an overuse injury of the <u>elbow</u>, especially the finger extensor <u>tendons</u> that originate in the <u>lateral</u> humeral epicondyle. Despite the term “epicondylitis,” there is no inflammation of the epicondyle; instead there is degeneration of the forearm <u>tendons</u>. [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)[[2]](/library/o6d0NI0)




### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[2]](/library/o6d0NI0)




* Most common in adults aged 40–60 years of age

* <u>♂</u> = <u>♀</u>





### Etiology




* Most commonly due to: [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)[[3]](/library/3OdSHJ0)

* Repeated or excessive <u>pronation</u>/<u>supination</u> and extension of the wrist (e.g., backhand shots in racket sports)

* Occupational activities (such as computer use)

* Can also be <u>idiopathic</u>





> [!NOTE]
> An EXTended game of tennis will ruin the Lawn: repeated EXTension of the <u>elbow</u> (e.g., in tennis) causes <u>lateral</u> epicondylitis.




### Clinical features [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)




* <u>Lateral</u> <u>elbow</u> <u>pain</u> [[2]](/library/o6d0NI0)

* <u>Pain</u> on extension of the wrist

* Reduced grip strength

* On examination, there is <u>pain</u> and tenderness over the <u>lateral epicondyle</u> and along extensor muscles. [[2]](/library/o6d0NI0)





### Diagnosis [[2]](/library/o6d0NI0)




* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u> based on history and provocation testing

* Provocation testing

* Cozen test (<u>tennis elbow test</u>) ;    [[4]](/library/K6dUNI0)[[5]](/library/66djNI0)

* The examiner holds the patient's hand with the thumb placed over the <u>lateral epicondyle</u>.

* The patient makes a fist, <u>pronates</u> the forearm, deviates radially, and extends the fist against the examiner's resistance.

* Test is positive if <u>pain</u> is elicited over the <u>lateral epicondyle</u>.

* Alternatives: <u>Mill test</u> or <u>Maudsley test</u>

* For diagnostic uncertainty: Consider imaging. [[6]](/library/uRdpKp0)

* Initial test: <u>x-ray</u> to exclude differential diagnoses

* Advanced imaging

* Modalities: <u>ultrasound</u> or <u>MRI</u> without contrast of the <u>elbow</u> [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)

* Findings: <u>tendon</u> thickening,irregular orientation of fibers





![Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow)](media/p92vscoosfn46u6r9ecishj9.jpg)

Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow)

![Lateral epicondylitis (common extensor tendinopathy)](media/nutp6xlxiafv86rdzkp00wnb.jpg)

Lateral epicondylitis (common extensor tendinopathy)




### Differential diagnoses of <u>lateral epicondylitis</u>[[2]](/library/o6d0NI0)




* <u>Osteoarthritis</u>

* <u>Radial tunnel syndrome</u>





### Management [[2]](/library/o6d0NI0)




* Advise patients that:

* Symptoms usually spontaneously resolve within 6–12 months.

* Using the affected limb normally will not cause damage.

* <u>Conservative management</u> is usually sufficient.

* For more information, see “<u>Management of insertional tendinopathies</u>.”

## Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow)

<u>Medial epicondylitis</u> is an overuse injury of the forearm, especially the finger flexor <u>tendons</u> that originate in the <u>medial epicondyle</u>. Despite the term “epicondylitis,” there is no inflammation of the epicondyle; instead there is degeneration of the forearm <u>tendons</u>. [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)[[7]](/library/ROdlHJ0)




### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[7]](/library/ROdlHJ0)[[8]](/library/Tpd6KI0)




* Most common between 30 and 50 years of age

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u>





### Etiology [[7]](/library/ROdlHJ0)




* Most commonly due to repeated wrist <u>flexion</u> and forearm <u>pronation</u> (e.g., playing golf or <u>overhead</u> throwing)

* Can also be <u>idiopathic</u>





> [!NOTE]
> A FLexible game of golf allows Mulligans: repeated FLexion of the <u>elbow</u> (e.g., in golf) causes <u>medial</u> epicondylitis.




### Clinical features [[7]](/library/ROdlHJ0)[[9]](/library/w6dhMI0)




* <u>Pain</u> in the <u>medial</u> <u>elbow</u> that radiates down the forearm (flexor muscles)

* Worsens with activity, particularly <u>flexion</u> of the wrist

* Reduced grip strength

* On examination, <u>pain</u> 5–10 mm <u>distal</u> and <u>anterior</u> to the epicondyle with possible <u>soft tissue</u> swelling [[7]](/library/ROdlHJ0)





### Diagnosis [[7]](/library/ROdlHJ0)[[10]](/library/96dNMI0)




* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u> based on history and provocation testing

* Provocation testing: <u>Pain</u> is elicited when the patient flexes the wrist against resistance, with the <u>elbow</u> held in extension.

* Consider assessing for <u>Tinel sign</u> to rule out coexistent ulnar <u>neuritis</u>.  [[7]](/library/ROdlHJ0)[[11]](/library/bqdHCI0)

* For diagnostic uncertainty: Consider imaging. [[6]](/library/uRdpKp0)

* Initial test: <u>x-ray</u>

* Excludes bone pathology

* Calcification of the common flexor tendor or ulnar collateral <u>ligament</u> is visible in up to 25% of patients. [[7]](/library/ROdlHJ0)

* Advanced imaging: <u>ultrasound</u> or <u>MRI</u> without contrast of the <u>elbow</u>





![Medial epicondylitis](media/qb4rz7i9ikf938rikx2m4fxs.jpg)

Medial epicondylitis




### Differential diagnoses [[7]](/library/ROdlHJ0)




* Ulnar <u>neuritis</u> (also a common coexisting condition)

* Ligamentous instability





### Management [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)[[7]](/library/ROdlHJ0)




* Most <u>medial epicondylitis</u> resolves with <u>conservative management</u>.

* Wrist <u>braces</u> may provide symptomatic relief.

* For more information, see “<u>Management of insertional tendinopathies</u>.”

## Iliotibial band syndrome

<u>Iliotibial band syndrome</u> is a common overuse injury of the <u>distal</u> portion of the <u>iliotibial band</u> (over the <u>lateral</u> femoral epicondyle).




### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* Occurs in up to 12% of runners [[12]](/library/Qidurp0)

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> [[13]](/library/eidxqp0)





### Etiology [[12]](/library/Qidurp0)




* Repetitive <u>flexion</u> and extension of the knee (e.g., from running, cycling)

* Inflammation may result from: [[14]](/library/hpdc6I0)

* Friction of band against <u>lateral</u> femoral condyle

* Compression of <u>connective tissue</u> and fat beneath the <u>iliotibial band</u>

* <u>Chronic inflammation</u> of the associated <u>bursa</u>





### Clinical features [[12]](/library/Qidurp0)




* <u>Pain</u> in the <u>lateral</u> knee (due to friction of <u>iliotibial band</u> against femoral epicondyle)

* Shooting <u>pain</u> immediately after the foot strikes the ground (may be accompanied by a snapping sensation)

* Dull, constant <u>pain</u> at rest

* Tenderness approximately 2 cm <u>proximal</u> to the <u>lateral</u> <u>joint</u> line [[15]](/library/uidptp0)

* Possible swelling at <u>distal</u> <u>iliotibial band</u>





### Diagnosis [[12]](/library/Qidurp0)[[15]](/library/uidptp0)




* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u> based on history and provocation testing

* Provocation tests

* Noble test  

* Patient lies on the unaffected side and flexes the affected knee to 90°.

* Examiner exerts constant pressure on the <u>lateral</u> femoral epicondyle while extending the knee.

* The test is positive if <u>pain</u> is elicited.

* Alternative: <u>Ober test</u>   [[12]](/library/Qidurp0)

* For refractory or recurrent <u>pain</u>: Obtain imaging.
* Initial test: <u>x-ray</u> to exclude differential diagnoses [[12]](/library/Qidurp0)[[16]](/library/CGWqYM0)





Advanced imaging: <u>MRI</u> without contrast   [[12]](/library/Qidurp0)




![Iliotibial band syndrome](media/l0o0achnt75vbw7ectnetdak.jpg)

Iliotibial band syndrome




### Differential diagnoses of iliotibial band syndrome [[12]](/library/Qidurp0)




* <u>Osteoarthritis of the knee</u>

* <u>Patellar maltracking</u>

* <u>Stress fractures</u>





### Management [[12]](/library/Qidurp0)[[15]](/library/uidptp0)




* Most patients recover fully after 6 weeks of <u>conservative management</u>.

* After initial rest, exercise therapy is recommended.

* <u>Surgery</u> may be required for persistent <u>pain</u>.

* For more information, see “<u>Management of insertional tendinopathies</u>.”

## Patellar tendonitis

<u>Patellar tendonitis</u> is an overuse injury of the <u>patellar tendon</u> at the <u>distal</u> portion of the patella. For information on <u>patellar tendon rupture</u>, see “<u>Sports injuries</u>.”




### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* Typically affects athletes [[17]](/library/OpdIpI0)

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> [[18]](/library/kpdmpI0)





### Etiology [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)




* Repeated jumping (e.g., volleyball, basketball)

* <u>Risk factors</u> include high <u>BMI</u>, <u>limb-length discrepancy</u>, and <u>pes planus</u>. [[19]](/library/ZpdZLI0)





### Clinical features [[18]](/library/kpdmpI0)




* Usually unilateral but can be bilateral

* <u>Pain</u> in the <u>anterior</u> aspect of the knee, localized to the inferior patella and <u>proximal</u> patella <u>tendon</u> [[19]](/library/ZpdZLI0)

* Symptoms worsen with knee <u>flexion</u> and prolonged activity.

* Tenderness when pressure is applied to the inferior border of the patella





### Diagnosis [[18]](/library/kpdmpI0)




* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u> based on history and provocation testing

* Provocation test: decline squat test [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)[[18]](/library/kpdmpI0)

* Patient performs a single leg squat on a board or block at a declined angle of 25°.

* If <u>pain</u> is reproduced, the test is positive.

* For refractory or recurrent <u>pain</u>: Obtain imaging. [[16]](/library/CGWqYM0)

* Initial test: <u>x-ray</u> (AP, <u>lateral</u>, <u>tangential patella view</u>) to exclude differential diagnoses

* Advanced imaging: <u>ultrasound</u> or <u>MRI</u> without contrast   [[18]](/library/kpdmpI0)





### Differential diagnoses of patellar tendonitis [[18]](/library/kpdmpI0)[[19]](/library/ZpdZLI0)




* <u>Osgood-Schlatter disease</u>

* <u>Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome</u>

* <u>Patellofemoral pain syndrome</u>

* <u>Meniscus tears</u>





### Management




* Initial management: <u>physical therapy</u> with <u>strength training</u> on a board or block at a declined angle [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)[[19]](/library/ZpdZLI0)

* For more information, see “<u>Management of insertional tendinopathies</u>.”

---

## Achilles tendinopathy

<u>Achilles tendinopathy</u> (achillodynia) is an overuse injury of the <u>Achilles tendon</u>. <u>Achilles tendon rupture</u> is discussed separately. [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)




### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[20]](/library/mpdVJI0)




* Most commonly affects individuals 30–60 years of age

* <u>♂</u> = <u>♀</u>





### Etiology [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)[[21]](/library/lidv7p0)




* Individuals (e.g., runners, other athletes) who have recently increased their exercise intensity

* Associated with <u>fluoroquinolone</u> use, especially in older adults [[22]](/library/PF1WRi0)





### Clinical features [[22]](/library/PF1WRi0)[[23]](/library/POdWsJ0)




* <u>Pain</u> with load-bearing activity

* Typically occurs in the morning or at the start of an exercise

* <u>Pain</u> that persists at rest often indicates chronic disease.

* Tenderness on palpation may be:

* At the insertion of the <u>Achilles tendon</u> (insertional tendinopathy)

* 2–6 cm above the insertion of the <u>Achilles tendon</u> (midportional tendinopathy)





### Diagnosis




* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u> based on history and provocation testing

* Provocation tests: performed with the patient lying <u>prone</u> with feet extending off the end of the examination table [[23]](/library/POdWsJ0)[[24]](/library/Npd-pI0)

* Arc sign

* The clinician palpates the thickened portion of the <u>tendon</u>.

* The patient <u>plantar flexes</u> and <u>dorsiflexes</u> the ankle.

* The test is positive when the thickened portion of <u>tendon</u> moves relative to the malleoli.

* Royal London test

* The clinician palpates to locate the point of tenderness, then passively <u>dorsiflexes</u> the patient's foot.

* The test is positive when <u>pain</u> decreases.

* For diagnostic uncertainty: Obtain imaging. [[25]](/library/Q61uk30)

* <u>Ultrasound</u>

* Initial study if there is high suspicion of Achilles pathology [[25]](/library/Q61uk30)

* Findings: <u>tendon</u> thickening [[22]](/library/PF1WRi0)

* <u>X-ray</u>

* Performed for heel <u>pain</u> of unknown origin [[25]](/library/Q61uk30)

* Findings: calcification at <u>tendon</u> insertion [[26]](/library/0pdeLI0)

* Advanced imaging: <u>MRI</u> without contrast [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)[[23]](/library/POdWsJ0)





### Differential diagnoses of <u>Achilles tendinopathy</u> [[21]](/library/lidv7p0)[[27]](/library/FJ1gD30)




* <u>Retrocalcaneal bursitis</u>

* <u>Haglund exostosis</u>

* Calcaneal apophysitis [[28]](/library/5pdiJI0) 

* Inflammation and <u>edema</u> secondary to a <u>stress fracture</u> of the <u>apophysis</u> of the <u>calcaneus</u>

* Causes heel <u>pain</u>, particularly on activity





### Management [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)[[23]](/library/POdWsJ0)




* Two-thirds of patients respond to <u>conservative management</u> with <u>physical therapy</u>.

* Avoid <u>corticosteroid</u> injections because of the risk of <u>tendon</u> rupture.

* For more information, see “<u>Management of insertional tendinopathies</u>.”

---

## Management

### <u>Conservative management</u> [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)[[15]](/library/uidptp0)




* <u>Relative rest</u>

* Ice

* Orthotic <u>braces</u>

* <u>Physical therapy</u>

* Topical or oral <u>NSAIDs</u> for 7–14 days (for dosages, see “<u>Analgesia</u>”) [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Physical therapy</u> includes <u>strength training</u> with appropriate <u>tendon</u> loading to promote <u>tendon</u> repair. [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)[[15]](/library/uidptp0)




### Refractory symptoms




* If <u>pain</u> persists for ≥ 3 months despite <u>conservative therapy</u>, consider referral to an orthopedic specialist.  [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)

* Noninvasive treatment options include:

* <u>Corticosteroid</u> injection

* <u>Platelet</u>-rich plasma injections

* Topical <u>nitroglycerin</u>

* <u>Extracorporeal shock wave therapy</u>

* Surgical options include:

* <u>Ultrasound</u>-guided <u>debridement</u>

* <u>Tendon</u> resection

* Open <u>debridement</u> [[29]](/library/HidKGp0)





> [!WARNING]
> Repeat <u>corticosteroid</u> injections may cause <u>tendon</u> rupture. [[1]](/library/vRdAKp0)
